Added in 4.12.0. `internal/backup` takes logical, table-data-only snapshots
of the historian and restores them. Off by default (`HOTLOOP_BACKUP_ENABLED`):
a deployment that has not configured a backup volume should not have this
process quietly writing into an ephemeral container filesystem.

## What this is

A snapshot of every row in every user-data table, taken over the same `pgx`
wire-protocol connection `internal/store` already uses, with PostgreSQL's
native `COPY table TO STDOUT` / `COPY table FROM STDIN`. A backup is a
directory: one file per table plus a small `manifest.json` (HotLoop version,
the schema migrations the database had applied, timestamp, and each table's
row count and columns with their types).

## What this is not

- **Not `pg_dump`/`pg_restore`.** The Gateway's runtime image
  (`gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot`) is deliberately a static
  binary and nothing else, no shell, no package manager, no external
  binaries of any kind. That is a design decision this feature does not get
  to override; see the `Containerfile`'s own header comment. Everything here
  goes over the same database connection the app already holds.
- **Not a schema backup.** `internal/store/migrations`, applied automatically
  by `store.Migrate` on every start (`HOTLOOP_DB_MIGRATE`, on by default),
  already reproduce the schema from nothing. A backup only ever captures
  table *data*, restoring one always assumes the schema will be rebuilt by
  migrations first, not by anything this package writes.
- **Not point-in-time recovery.** There is no WAL archiving and no
  continuous replication here. A backup is a snapshot at the moment it ran;
  anything written after that moment and before the next backup is not
  covered.
- **Not off-box storage.** The backup directory (`HOTLOOP_BACKUP_DIR`,
  meant to be backed by the `backup.persistence` PVC this chart provisions)
  is still a single volume in the same cluster. Getting backups onto
  genuinely durable, replicated, or offline storage, copying the volume
  to object storage, snapshotting the PVC, whatever an operator's actual
  infrastructure provides, is the operator's job, the same way this
  project already treats durable storage as infrastructure's responsibility
  rather than something the app reinvents a multi-cloud backend adapter for.

## Protect the backup files

Backup files are sensitive. The `users.copy` file holds bcrypt password
hashes, and `sessions.copy` and `write_audit.copy` hold session records and the
write audit trail. Files are created with mode `0640` (and the backup
directory `0750`), and a pre-existing file is an error rather than
overwritten, but that is a floor, not a substitute for protecting the volume:
keep the backup volume on encrypted-at-rest storage, restrict who and what can
read it, and apply the same care to any off-box copy an operator makes.

The `devices.copy` file holds each device's address and protocol configuration as
they are stored, which includes the credentials the drivers log in with. How
readable they are depends on the key, below. Since 4.15.1 the API hides every
device credential from every role, admin included; a backup file is not behind
the API. See [AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/#where-credentials-are-still-in-the-clear).

## Device credentials and the secret key

A backup is the file that gets copied to a laptop, a share and a ticket. So the
credentials in it are encrypted, with a key that is never in the database and
never in a backup.

- **With `HOTLOOP_SECRET_KEY_FILE` set** (the chart sets it, with a key it
  generates on install and keeps across upgrades and uninstalls), every keyed
  credential (the `password` of OPC UA, MQTT, HTTP, MTConnect and UniFi devices,
  HTTP and MTConnect header values such as API keys, the password of each
  other MQTT broker discovery listens to, and the password of each historian
  target) is encrypted in the database, and `devices.copy`, `mqtt_sources.copy`
  and `historian_targets.copy` hold the ciphertext. The manifest lists the key it was
  encrypted with as `secretKeyIds`: an id, never the key.
- **Without it**, those credentials are in the database and in `devices.copy` in
  the clear, and HotLoop says so in its startup log. UniFi consoles, MQTT
  brokers with a password and historian targets with a password can't be saved
  at all without a key. Set one and restart: everything already stored is
  encrypted at that start.
- **Either way**, a credential written into a URL (`mqtt://user:pass@host`, a
  `?token=` query value) or into free text such as an HTTP body stays in the
  clear. Put it in the `password` option instead.

**Restoring needs the same key.** `--restore-from` checks the manifest before it
loads a row: a backup encrypted with a key the restoring HotLoop does not have is
refused, and the error names the key it needs. Restore with that key file mounted.
If the key is gone for good, add `--restore-keep-unreadable-credentials`:
everything else comes back, and each device whose credential can't be opened stays
down, saying which key it needs, until somebody enters the credential again. A
backup taken before there was a key restores anywhere, and its credentials are
encrypted as soon as the restore finishes.

**Keep the key somewhere the backup isn't.** A key stored next to its backups
protects nothing. With the chart it's the `<release>-secret-key` Secret; back
that up the way you back up the rest of the cluster's secrets, separately.

## Why `COPY table TO STDOUT` alone does not work

The obvious approach, issue `COPY table_name TO STDOUT` for each table and
stream the result to a file, was tried against a real
`timescale/timescaledb:2.29.1-pg16` instance while building this feature, and
it is actively wrong, not just less general:

- Against `tag_history` when it is a **TimescaleDB hypertable**, that exact
  statement does not error. It answers with a `NOTICE`
  ("hypertable data are in the chunks, no data will be copied") and copies
  **zero rows**. A backup built this way "succeeds" and is silently empty
  for exactly the table this project cares most about not losing.
- Against `tag_history` when it is the **native-partitioning fallback** (a
  plain table declared `PARTITION BY RANGE`, used when TimescaleDB is not
  available), the same statement fails outright:
  `ERROR: cannot copy from partitioned table`.

Postgres's own hint in the second case is the fix `internal/backup` uses for
every table, unconditionally, hypertable or not, partitioned or not:

```sql
COPY (SELECT * FROM tag_history) TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT binary)
```

Verified against the same instance: this form reads every row across all of
a hypertable's chunks, or all of a partitioned table's partitions,
transparently and correctly, no need to enumerate chunk or partition tables
by name. This codebase uses neither compressed hypertables nor continuous
aggregates (see `internal/store/migrations` and `internal/store/migrate.go`, `tag_history` is a plain hypertable or a plain range-partitioned table,
nothing more exotic), so neither of those features' additional COPY caveats
apply here.

`COPY table FROM STDIN`, used for restore, needs no such rewrite: it always
names a table, never a query, and both TimescaleDB and Postgres's native
partitioning route an incoming row to the correct chunk or partition exactly
as an ordinary `INSERT` would, also verified against the same instance.

## What is backed up, and in what order

Every user-data table, in foreign-key dependency order (a table always comes
after every table its own foreign keys point to):

```
devices → tags → tag_latest → alarm_definitions → alarm_state →
alarm_events → automations → automation_runs → blueprints → scripts → script_runs →
recipes → recipe_versions → recipe_applications → events → write_audit →
settings → users → sessions → fleet_members → report_definitions →
report_runs → entity_state_log → tag_history
```

(Abridged; `backup.Tables` is the whole list, the entity and equipment tables
and `entity_last_state` included.) The logbook's `entity_state_log` is
partitioned by month in both history modes and goes just before
`tag_history`, the only table larger. A restore loads its rows before any of
its monthly partitions exist, so they land in its default partition. The
logbook's maintenance, when a recording Gateway starts, makes last month's and
this month's partitions around the rows that belong in them, and deletes older
rows from the default partition as they pass the retention, so the retention
reaches every restored row. See [LOGBOOK.md](/iot/logbook/).

Scripts come back with their history. A run the backup caught in the middle
comes back `running`, and the Gateway's first start marks it cancelled,
`interrupted by restart`, the same as a run a crash cut off: nothing resumes
a run. See [SCRIPTS.md](/iot/scripts/).

Recipes come back with every version and every application. An application
the backup caught halfway comes back `applying`, and the Gateway's first start
marks it `failed`, pointing at its call id in the write audit: nothing resumes
one, and nothing undoes one. See [RECIPES.md](/iot/recipes/).

`schema_migrations` is deliberately excluded: `store.Migrate` rebuilds it,
and every table's DDL, from the embedded migrations. It is the one entry in
`backup.ExcludedTables`, which records why each excluded table is excluded.

The list is kept by hand, which is how a table can be added by a migration and
silently left out of every backup afterward. Two tests guard against it, and
both run against a real database in both storage modes.
`TestEveryTableIsBackedUpOrExcluded` reads the tables that exist from
`information_schema` and fails if any is in neither `Tables` nor
`ExcludedTables`, naming it. `TestTablesAreInForeignKeyOrder` reads the foreign
keys from the database and fails if a table is listed before one it references.
The scheduled-reports tables (`report_definitions`, `report_runs`) are the first
tables added under these guards. The reports' output files are on the reports
volume and are not part of a database backup. `tag_history` is loaded
last on restore, it has no foreign key of its own and is by a wide margin
the largest table, so every small configuration table fails fast, if it is
going to fail at all, before that one long step even starts.

**`settings` has one deliberate exception.** The `history_mode` row is
written by `store.ensureHistorySchema` itself, once, the moment `Migrate`
builds a schema from nothing, it records whether *this server* built
`tag_history` as a TimescaleDB hypertable or a natively partitioned table,
which is a fact about the database `Migrate` just ran against, not a fact
about the plant. It is excluded from both the backup and the restore of
`settings`: restoring a source install's historical decision onto a target
whose capabilities differ (or even just onto a fresh `Migrate` run against
the very same class of server) could rewrite this row to describe a shape
the target does not actually have. The target's own `Migrate` has already
made the right call before `Restore` ever looks at `settings`, and that call
is left alone.

## On-demand backups

- `POST /api/backup` (`backup.run`, admin-only) takes a backup right now and
  returns the manifest.
- `GET /api/backup` (`backup.read`, admin-only) lists what is on the backup
  volume: name, size on disk, and the manifest (table list, row counts,
  HotLoop version, timestamp) for each one.

Both are admin-only by omission from the operator role, the same narrowing
`fleet.restart`/`fleet.config`/`notify.test` already apply to other
operational, "do it now" or administratively-scoped actions. A backup
listing's row counts, including `users` and `sessions`, read closer to an
administrative diagnostic than to the plant-floor reads (devices, tags,
alarms) the operator role is meant to see, so `backup.read` was not split
out to a lower permission the way some reads are; that is a judgment call,
not a technical constraint, and could be revisited if a real operator
workflow needs it.

## Scheduling and retention

`HOTLOOP_BACKUP_INTERVAL` (e.g. `24h`) runs a backup on a fixed tick. This is
deliberately a plain interval, not a cron expression parser, the realistic
need is "back this up every so often," and this project's own convention is
not to build for a need nobody has yet. Leaving it unset (or `0`) disables
the scheduler; the on-demand endpoint still works, for an operator or an
external cron who would rather trigger it themselves.

`HOTLOOP_BACKUP_RETAIN` (default `7`) keeps the newest N backup directories,
deleting older ones after every successful backup. `0` or less keeps
everything, a choice an operator has to make deliberately on a small
volume.

## Restoring a backup

**Restore is deliberately not an API endpoint.** Automating "restore now" as
a live, network-triggerable action against a database that may be serving
production traffic is a real hazard, one wrong click, or one compromised
admin session, overwrites live data, that this project is not building
without being explicitly asked to. Restore is a flag on the binary itself,
run once, by hand, by an operator who has already decided the target
database is meant to receive it:

```sh
hotloop --restore-from=/data/backups/20260918T220000Z
```

What this does, in order:

1. Loads configuration and connects to the database exactly like an
   ordinary start, `store.Open` runs the same migrations, building the
   schema restore is about to load data into.
2. **Refuses a backup it cannot load without losing something**: one taken at
   a newer schema than this database's, or one with a table or column this
   version no longer has. Both are checked before a single row is loaded. See
   "Restoring onto a different version" below.
3. **Refuses if any target table already has data** beyond what `Migrate`
   itself just seeded (the one `history_mode` row in `settings`), restore only ever runs against a database with nothing in it yet. This is
   the safety check: a table with even one existing row stops the whole
   restore before any `COPY FROM STDIN` runs.
4. Loads every table, in dependency order, inside a single transaction, into
   the columns the manifest names.
5. Resets the backing sequence for every table with a `bigserial` primary
   key (`tags`, `alarm_events`, `automation_runs`, `events`, `write_audit`,
   `sessions`) to one past the highest restored id, `COPY FROM STDIN` loads
   explicit id values without touching the sequence, so skipping this would
   leave the very next ordinary insert colliding with a restored row.
6. Re-counts every table and compares against the manifest's row counts,
   inside the same still-open transaction.
7. Commits only if every count matched. A mismatch, or any error at any
   earlier step, rolls the whole transaction back, leaving the target
   database exactly as empty as it was found, never partially loaded.
8. Exits. Nothing else in the process starts: no poll scheduler, no alarm
   engine, no API server. A restore has no use for any of them, and starting
   the runtime against a database mid-restore would be its own hazard.

### Restoring onto a different version

The release you restore with is rarely the release that took the backup. The
backup was taken months ago on whatever was running then, and the box you are
rebuilding runs today's. So here is what restores onto what.

**An older backup onto a newer HotLoop: yes.** That is the case that matters,
and it is tested from every schema level there has been, `0001_core` through
today, on TimescaleDB and on plain PostgreSQL, with the app started afterward.

- Every manifest records each table's columns, names and types. Restore loads
  each file into exactly those columns, by name. A column added since the
  backup takes its default. `write_audit`'s `entity_id`, `service` and
  `call_id` come back empty on every audit row from before entity services,
  which is what those rows were: plain tag writes.
- A table added since the backup stays empty, and the app fills what it can
  when it starts. The entity registry's first sync gives every restored tag
  its read entity, every armed tag its control entity and every alarm
  definition its alarm entity, with the names the registry would have given
  them. Devices from a backup older than the equipment tree get placed on it
  by their site, area and line text during the restore itself, the same way
  the upgrade placed them. What was never in the backup can't come back:
  labels, composite entities, and entity names an operator customised after
  the backup was taken.

**A newer backup onto an older HotLoop: no, refused.** The manifest records
every migration the backup's database had applied. If it has one this
database has never run, restore stops before loading a row and says so:

```
refusing to restore: this backup was taken by HotLoop <its version> with the
database schema at <its newest migration>, which is newer than this database's
schema at <this database's newest migration> (HotLoop <this version>). ...
Restore it with HotLoop <its version> or a later release
```

"Newer" means migrations, not version strings. A version string says which
binary took the backup, and dev builds, release candidates and hotfix branches
make comparing those a guess. The migrations say what the schema actually was,
and they're compared as a set, so a missing migration is caught wherever it
falls in the order. The versions are in the message because the version is
what you can act on: which release to restore with.

**A backup with a column this version no longer has: refused, by name.** The
day a migration drops, renames or retypes a column, a backup from before it has
data the new table has no place for. Restore won't guess. It names every such
column, across every table, before loading anything:

- a column the running table doesn't have is refused, unless
  `backup.columnRenames` maps it to its new name. A migration that renames a
  column adds that entry, and a test restoring a backup from before it, in the
  same change. There are no renames today, so the map is empty;
- a column whose type changed is refused. Binary COPY carries no types, so the
  bytes would be read as the new type or rejected halfway through;
- a column the running table has added as `NOT NULL` with no default is
  refused, because nothing could fill it.

The way out is the same for all three: restore with the release that took the
backup, then upgrade that database in place, which is how the migration was
meant to meet that data.

Loading by name also covers the change nobody notices: a column dropped and
re-added, or a table rebuilt, so the columns sit in a different order. Loading
by position would put one column's values into another's without an error
whenever the types line up. By name, each lands where it belongs.

**Backups taken before manifests recorded any of this** (every backup made
before this release) have no column lists and no schema. They still restore:

- Without column lists, restore falls back to position. A file with fewer
  columns than the table goes into the table's first columns, and the rest
  take their defaults. That is right for every schema so far, because every
  migration to date only added columns, and `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` always
  appends. A file with more columns than the table is refused by PostgreSQL
  itself.
- Without a schema, restore assumes the backup is as new as it could possibly
  be: `0007_service_audit.sql`, the newest migration there was when manifests
  started recording it. That assumption can only ever refuse a restore that
  would have worked, never let through one that wouldn't. In practice it
  refuses nothing, because any HotLoop with this check has already run every
  migration up to that one.

The first backup this release takes records everything, so the fallback only
matters for backups already sitting on a backup volume.

### Restore procedure, step by step

1. Get the backup directory onto the machine or volume the target
   deployment's `hotloop` binary can read, this is the point where an
   operator's own off-box copy of the backup volume comes back into play.
2. Point `HOTLOOP_DB_*` at the **target** database. It must be reachable and
   have no data yet in any of the tables `internal/backup.Tables` lists (a
   brand new, empty database is the normal case; `store.Migrate` will build
   the schema in step 3).
3. Run `hotloop --restore-from=<path to the backup directory>`.
4. Read the final log line: `restore complete` with the table and row
   counts, or an error explaining exactly what was refused and why.
5. Start `hotloop` normally against that same database.

## Moving between databases

A backup is the same thing whatever database took it: PostgreSQL's binary
COPY files and a manifest that names every column's Postgres type. On SQLite
there's no COPY, so `internal/backup` writes those same bytes itself, with
pgx's own encoders, and reads them back the same way. So moving a plant from
one database to another is a backup on the old one and a restore into the new
one. Nothing else.

- **SQLite to Postgres or TimescaleDB.** The Pi that outgrew its file. Take a
  backup, point `HOTLOOP_DB_*` at the new server (`HOTLOOP_DB_TYPE=postgres`),
  restore. On a TimescaleDB server the history lands in a hypertable.
- **Postgres or TimescaleDB to SQLite.** A plant going down onto a small box.
  Same thing the other way, with `HOTLOOP_DB_TYPE=sqlite`.
- **Plain Postgres to TimescaleDB, and back.** The history mode is sticky, so
  pointing a Gateway at an IoT box's plain Postgres keeps its partitions. To
  get a hypertable, restore into a fresh TimescaleDB. Going the other way gets
  you partitions.

What's checked on the way in is what's checked for any restore: every column
by name and type against the target, with SQLite's columns read as their
Postgres types, so a backup from one restores into the other or refuses for
the same reason it would anywhere. `history_mode` is never copied: the target
keeps what its own migrations decided. Sequences come out right on both: on
Postgres `fixSequences` moves them, and SQLite's AUTOINCREMENT moves itself
past any id restored into it.

`TestRestoreMovesBetweenDatabases` does each of these for real: SQLite to
Postgres and back, partitions to a hypertable and back, every table seeded,
backed up, restored and checked value by value.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_BACKUP_ENABLED` | `false` | The feature is off, including the API routes, until this is set |
| `HOTLOOP_BACKUP_DIR` | `/data/backups` | Where backups are written; meant to be a PVC (`backup.persistence` in the chart) |
| `HOTLOOP_BACKUP_RETAIN` | `7` | Newest N backups kept; `0` or less keeps everything |
| `HOTLOOP_BACKUP_INTERVAL` | unset | e.g. `24h`; unset means on-demand only |

`--restore-from=<dir>` is a `cmd/hotloop` flag, not an environment variable, see "Restoring a backup" above.

## What has and has not been verified

**Verified**, not merely tested, see this repository's own distinction
between the two, and the reasoning below for why that distinction mattered
here specifically.

The real risk with a backup/restore feature is a test suite that proves a
file was created without proving the data in it is actually recoverable, exactly the shape of the two real bugs caught in the two PRs immediately
before this one (an SMTP channel whose tests all passed against an
unauthenticated relay while the authenticated path was silently broken; a
genuine data race caught only because the race detector was actually run,
not skipped). So the test that matters here is the full round trip, run
against a real `timescale/timescaledb:2.29.1-pg16` instance:

- Write real data through the normal store API, a device, a tag, a tag
  reading (`tag_latest` and `tag_history` both), an alarm definition with
  live state and a recorded event, an automation with a finished run, a
  system event, a write-audit row, a custom setting, a user with a session,
  a fleet member.
- Back it up.
- Stand up a **second, independently created and migrated, genuinely empty**
  database, not the source database wiped in place.
- Restore into it.
- Assert the restored **values** match what was written, not just that row
  counts line up: the device's name and address, the tag's scale, the exact
  history reading, the alarm's state and trip value, the alarm event, the
  automation and its run's status, the custom setting, the user's role, the
  session, the fleet member.
- Assert `history_mode` in the restored database reflects what *that
  database's own* `Migrate` decided, not the source's recorded value.
- Assert the sequence fix actually works: insert a new row into a restored
  `bigserial` table after the restore and confirm it neither collides with
  a restored id nor errors.
- Assert the safety check actually refuses: attempting to restore into a
  database that still holds the original seeded data fails with an error
  naming the problem, and the original data is provably untouched
  afterward.
- Retention (`Prune`) and listing (`List`) are exercised directly at the
  filesystem level: the newest N backups survive, older ones are deleted,
  and a listing reports them newest-first with the right row counts.
- The interval scheduler (`Manager.tick`) is exercised end to end against a
  real database, started, left to tick more than once, stopped, and this
  is also the test the race detector was run against
  (`go test ./internal/backup/... -race -count=10`, inside a `golang:1.26`
  container, since this development machine has no cgo compiler) for ten
  iterations with no races reported.
- `POST /api/backup` and `GET /api/backup` were exercised against a real
  running `hotloop` instance, not only through `go test`.

**Not verified**: behavior under a `tag_history` large enough that a single
backup or restore takes so long the surrounding transaction becomes a
practical concern (lock contention, connection pool exhaustion under
concurrent normal traffic), the round-trip test's data volumes are small by
design, since what it needs to prove is correctness, not throughput.

Restoring across versions is tested, not assumed. `TestRestoreFromEverySchemaLevel`
builds a database the way each release left it, migration by migration with
data written at each step, takes the backup that release would have taken, and
restores it onto today's schema twice: once with today's manifest and once with
the manifest every earlier release wrote. Then it starts the runtime, the alarm
engine and the entity registry, the way the app does, and checks the device is
on the tree, every tag and the alarm have an entity, an operator's entity name
survived, and the audit rows are intact with the newer columns empty. It runs on
TimescaleDB and on plain PostgreSQL. `TestRestoreRefusesABackupFromANewerSchema`
restores today's backup onto a database whose schema stops at
`0005_entities.sql` and checks it's refused with both versions and both schema
levels in the message and nothing loaded. `TestRestoreMatchesColumnsByName`
applies a test-only migration to a throwaway database (a reordered column, a
dropped one, a renamed one with and without a mapping, a retyped one, a new
`NOT NULL` one) and checks each loads correctly or is refused by name. A
renamed column with no mapping, a dropped one and a retyped one are refused
rather than handled: see "Restoring onto a different version".
